stimulus.content: Night trains are returning to Europe. For two decades they were cut back as budget airlines took over long-distance travel, and by 2015 most cross-border sleeper routes had closed. Rising concern about aviation emissions changed the calculation. A traveller who boards in Vienna at nine in the evening and steps off in Amsterdam after breakfast has spent no daytime hours in transit and released a fraction of the carbon a flight would have cost. Several operators have since ordered new sleeper carriages, the first such orders in a generation.

stem: According to the passage, why were night trains cut back before 2015?

choices.text: Passengers preferred to travel during the day.
The carriages had become unsafe to operate.
Governments withdrew rail funding entirely.
Budget airlines took over long-distance travel.
Cross-border agreements expired.

explanation:
The second sentence states it directly: services were cut back «as budget airlines took over long-distance travel».

The other options name plausible-sounding reasons that the passage never mentions.

distractorRationale.A: The passage argues the opposite — overnight travel saves daytime hours.
distractorRationale.B: Safety is never raised in the passage.
distractorRationale.C: No mention is made of funding being withdrawn.

explanation:

distractorRationale.D: No prices appear anywhere in the passage.
distractorRationale.E: Neither city is recommended as a destination; they simply mark the route.

stimulus.content: Coral reefs cover a tiny share of the ocean floor yet shelter about a quarter of all marine fish species. Their branching structures create hiding places for young fish and surfaces on which countless smaller organisms live. Reefs also absorb wave energy before it reaches the shore, which reduces coastal erosion during storms. Where reefs have died, communities have had to build sea walls that cost far more to maintain than the reef cost to protect.

stem: According to the passage, reefs reduce coastal erosion by ...

choices.text: growing on top of sea walls
supporting smaller organisms
covering a large share of the ocean floor
absorbing wave energy before it reaches the shore
sheltering young fish

explanation: The third sentence gives the mechanism directly: reefs «absorb wave energy before it reaches the shore, which reduces coastal erosion during storms».

distractorRationale.A: The passage says sea walls replace lost reefs, not that reefs grow on them.
distractorRationale.B: Another real function, again unrelated to erosion.
distractorRationale.C: The passage says reefs cover only a tiny share.
distractorRationale.E: A real function of reefs, but unrelated to erosion.

explanation:

That is a common move in environmental writing: an argument becomes harder to dismiss once its cost is stated.

distractorRationale.A: The sentence reports what communities have had to do, without arguing against it.
distractorRationale.D: No description of a dead reef appears.

stimulus.content: Handwriting is disappearing from many classrooms, replaced by typing from the earliest years. Studies comparing the two find that students who write notes by hand recall more of what they heard, even though typists capture more words. The likely reason is that handwriting is slower: unable to record everything, the writer must decide what matters and phrase it in their own words. Typing fast enough to transcribe verbatim removes that decision, and with it the thinking the decision required.

stem: According to the passage, students who type capture ...

choices.text: nothing that is worth reviewing later
more words but remember less
the same number of words as handwriters
only the main ideas of a lecture
fewer words but remember more

explanation:
The second sentence states both halves: handwriters «recall more of what they heard, even though typists capture more words».

The two measures point in opposite directions, and that is precisely the passage's point.

distractorRationale.A: The passage never dismisses typed notes as worthless.
distractorRationale.C: The passage says typists capture more.
distractorRationale.D: Capturing main ideas describes the handwriters' approach.
distractorRationale.E: This reverses the finding; handwriters record fewer words.

stem: According to the passage, the advantage of handwriting comes from ...

choices.text: the greater number of words recorded

explanation:
The third sentence names the mechanism: because handwriting cannot keep up, the writer must choose what matters and put it in their own words. That selecting and rephrasing is the thinking that aids recall.

Note the passage credits the constraint, not the medium itself — a distinction that matters if one asks how to get the same benefit while typing.

distractorRationale.A: Handwriters record fewer words, not more.
distractorRationale.D: Physical movement is not offered as the explanation.

stem: Which recommendation follows most directly from the passage's reasoning?

choices.text: Note-taking should be abandoned altogether.
Lectures should be delivered more slowly.
Students should be graded on handwriting neatness.
Students who type should be asked to summarise rather than transcribe.
Laptops should be banned from all classrooms.

explanation:
The passage locates the benefit in selecting and rephrasing, not in the pen itself. If that is right, the benefit can be recovered on a keyboard by requiring summary instead of verbatim capture.

Banning laptops would also work, but it treats the tool as the cause when the passage points to the habit — and it discards the advantages typing has.

distractorRationale.A: The passage treats note-taking as valuable throughout.
distractorRationale.B: Slowing lectures does not restore the act of choosing what to record.
distractorRationale.C: Neatness has no bearing on the mechanism described.
distractorRationale.E: Addresses the tool rather than the habit the passage identifies as decisive.

stimulus.content: The first public libraries were not built to lend books. They were built to keep them. Volumes were rare and costly, so early collections chained each book to its shelf and readers stood to read. Lending began only when printing made replacement affordable — that is, when losing a book stopped being a catastrophe. The chains came off not because librarians grew trusting, but because the arithmetic changed.

stem: According to the passage, early library books were chained because ...

choices.text: readers were known to be dishonest

explanation:
The third sentence gives the reason: «Volumes were rare and costly, so early collections chained each book to its shelf.»

The final sentence reinforces it by ruling out the alternative explanation — the chains were about cost, not about trust.

distractorRationale.A: The passage explicitly denies that trust was the issue.
distractorRationale.C: The passage says lending began when printing made replacement affordable, not that printing was unknown.
distractorRationale.D: Standing was a consequence of chaining, not its purpose.

distractorRationale.B: The scales stayed boxed in the cupboard.
